questions.prompt: An even-parity scheme appends one parity bit to data bits 1011010. What parity bit is appended?
options: Either value
No parity bit is needed
questions.explanation: The data contains four 1s, already an even count. Appending 0 preserves even parity.

questions.prompt: How many 1 bits are in the odd-parity codeword 11010101, including its parity bit?
questions.explanation: The bit string contains five 1s, which is odd as required by odd parity.

questions.prompt: Which error patterns are guaranteed to be detected by a single parity bit?
answer: Any single-bit error
Any odd number of bit errors
questions.explanation: Parity changes when an odd number of bits flip, so all odd-weight error patterns are detected. Even numbers of flips preserve parity and may go undetected.
options: Any single-bit error
Any odd number of bit errors
A single parity bit detects every even number of bit errors
A single parity bit detects every burst error of length at most two

questions.prompt: A code has minimum Hamming distance d_min=5. What is the maximum number of errors it can guarantee to correct?
questions.explanation: A code with minimum distance d can correct at most floor((d−1)/2) errors. For d=5, this is floor(4/2)=2.

questions.prompt: A code has minimum distance 6. How many bit errors can it guarantee to detect?
questions.explanation: A code with minimum distance d detects up to d−1 errors. Here 6−1=5 errors are guaranteed detectable.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Hamming distance are correct?
answer: It counts bit positions in which two equal-length strings differ
Minimum distance d can detect up to d−1 errors
Minimum distance d can correct floor((d−1)/2) errors
questions.explanation: Detection requires a corrupted word not to become another codeword; correction requires disjoint radius-t neighborhoods. For d=4, guaranteed correction is only floor(3/2)=1 error.
options: It counts bit positions in which two equal-length strings differ
Minimum distance d can detect up to d−1 errors
Minimum distance d can correct floor((d−1)/2) errors
Minimum distance d can correct d-1 errors

questions.prompt: A CRC uses generator polynomial G(x)=x^3+x+1. How many zero bits are appended to the data before division?
questions.explanation: The generator degree is three. CRC encoding appends r=3 zeros before division to obtain a three-bit remainder.

questions.prompt: Using generator 1011, find the 3-bit CRC remainder for data 1101. Use modulo-2 division of 1101000 by 1011.
questions.explanation: Modulo-2 long division of 1101000 by 1011 leaves remainder 001. The transmitted codeword is 1101001.

questions.prompt: A CRC generator has degree r. Which burst-error guarantee is standard?
options: All burst errors of length at most r are detected
Only single-bit errors are detected
No burst error can be detected
All errors of any length are detected
answer: All burst errors of length at most r are detected
questions.explanation: A degree-r CRC detects every burst error whose length is at most r. Longer bursts are detected with high probability but are not all guaranteed to be detected.

questions.prompt: Which statements about CRC error detection are correct?
answer: The receiver divides the received codeword by the agreed generator
A zero remainder is consistent with no detected error
CRC can detect all burst errors shorter than the generator degree
questions.explanation: A zero syndrome means the received polynomial is divisible by the generator, but some error patterns may be undetected. CRC guarantees detection of bursts up to its degree.
options: The receiver divides the received codeword by the agreed generator
A zero remainder is consistent with no detected error
CRC can detect all burst errors shorter than the generator degree
A zero remainder proves that the transmitted frame was error-free

questions.prompt: A byte-oriented framing protocol uses byte stuffing. If the payload contains the same byte as the frame delimiter, what does the sender do?
options: Escape or stuff the delimiter occurrence in the payload
Delete the payload byte
Treat it as the end of frame
Restart the physical link
answer: Escape or stuff the delimiter occurrence in the payload
questions.explanation: Byte stuffing inserts an escape sequence so a delimiter-valued payload byte is not mistaken for a frame boundary.

questions.prompt: Which statements about bit stuffing are correct?
answer: The sender inserts a 0 after a run of five consecutive 1s in common HDLC-style framing
The receiver removes the inserted 0
It allows flag patterns to appear in data without ending the frame
questions.explanation: Bit stuffing prevents the flag sequence from appearing in the transmitted data stream. The receiver destuffs the bits, recovering the original payload.
options: The sender inserts a 0 after a run of five consecutive 1s in common HDLC-style framing
The receiver removes the inserted 0
It allows flag patterns to appear in data without ending the frame
The receiver inserts a 0 after five consecutive 1s

questions.prompt: Bit stuffing inserts one 0 after every run of five consecutive 1s. How many bits are transmitted for payload 11111011, excluding flags?
questions.explanation: A stuffed 0 follows the first five 1s. The original payload has 8 bits, so one inserted bit makes 9 transmitted bits.

questions.prompt: A framing method uses a fixed-size frame with a length field. What is a principal advantage over delimiter-only framing?
options: The receiver can determine the frame boundary from the specified length
It eliminates all header overhead
It detects every transmission error
It needs no synchronization
answer: The receiver can determine the frame boundary from the specified length
questions.explanation: A length field tells the receiver how many bytes belong to the frame, allowing boundary recovery without relying solely on a delimiter value.

questions.prompt: Which techniques can be used to delineate frames on a bit stream?
answer: Length fields
Sentinel flags with bit stuffing
Byte delimiters with byte stuffing
questions.explanation: Length fields and escaped delimiters or flags provide frame boundaries. Routing tables choose packet paths and do not delimit link frames.
options: Length fields
Sentinel flags with bit stuffing
Byte delimiters with byte stuffing
Preamble bits alone identify every frame boundary on an arbitrary bit stream

questions.prompt: In stop-and-wait ARQ, why is a sequence number needed even if only one data frame is outstanding?
options: To distinguish a retransmitted duplicate from a new frame
To choose the physical transmission rate
To route the frame across networks
To calculate the frame checksum
answer: To distinguish a retransmitted duplicate from a new frame
questions.explanation: If an ACK is lost, the sender retransmits the same frame. A sequence number lets the receiver recognize and discard the duplicate instead of delivering data twice.

questions.prompt: Stop-and-wait uses 1000-bit data frames on a 1 Mb/s link. The round-trip propagation and ACK time is 19 ms, and ACK transmission is negligible. What is utilization, as a percentage, ignoring processing?
questions.explanation: Data transmission takes 1 ms. One cycle is 1+19=20 ms, so utilization is 1/20=0.05=5%.

questions.prompt: A stop-and-wait sender transmits a frame and receives no ACK before timeout. What is the normal response?
options: Retransmit the outstanding frame
Discard all future frames permanently
Increase the sequence number and skip the data
Send an Ethernet broadcast
answer: Retransmit the outstanding frame
questions.explanation: A timeout indicates the frame or its acknowledgment may have been lost. Stop-and-wait ARQ retransmits the unacknowledged frame.

questions.prompt: Which events can cause a stop-and-wait ARQ retransmission?
answer: The data frame is corrupted
The data frame is lost
The ACK is lost
questions.explanation: Loss or corruption prevents the sender from receiving a valid acknowledgment. A lost ACK can cause a duplicate retransmission even though the receiver accepted the original frame.
options: The data frame is corrupted
The data frame is lost
The ACK is lost
A lost ACK always proves that the original data frame was lost

questions.prompt: A data-link frame transmission succeeds independently with probability 0.9 on each attempt. With unlimited retries, what is the expected number of attempts per delivered frame?
questions.explanation: The number of attempts is geometric with success probability 0.9. Its expectation is 1/0.9?1.111 attempts per successfully delivered frame.

questions.prompt: For a sliding-window protocol with m-bit sequence numbers, what is the maximum sender window for Go-Back-N?
questions.explanation: Go-Back-N reserves one sequence-number value to distinguish the oldest unacknowledged frame from a new frame after wraparound. Its sender window is at most 2^m−1.

questions.prompt: For Selective Repeat ARQ with m-bit sequence numbers, what is the largest safe sender window?
options: m
questions.explanation: Selective Repeat allows the receiver to buffer out-of-order frames. To avoid ambiguity after sequence-number wraparound, its window must be at most half the sequence space.

questions.prompt: A Go-Back-N sender has frames 5, 6, and 7 outstanding. It receives a cumulative ACK indicating that frame 6 is next expected, then the timer for the oldest unacknowledged frame expires. Which frames are retransmitted?
answer: 6 and 7
questions.explanation: The ACK confirms that frame 5 arrived, leaving 6 and 7 outstanding. Go-Back-N retransmits the missing frame and every later outstanding frame after a timeout.
options: 6 and 7
Only 5
Only 7

questions.prompt: A Selective Repeat receiver expects sequence number 5 and receives a valid frame 6 first. What is the usual action?
answer: Buffer frame 6 and acknowledge it, but wait to deliver in order
questions.explanation: Selective Repeat accepts and buffers an in-window out-of-order frame. It can acknowledge frame 6 individually, but ordered delivery waits until frame 5 arrives.
options: Buffer frame 6 and acknowledge it, but wait to deliver in order
Discard frame 6 and acknowledge only frame 5
Deliver frame 6 immediately as the next application bytes
Reset the sequence space

questions.prompt: Which statements distinguish Go-Back-N from Selective Repeat?
answer: Go-Back-N may retransmit multiple frames after one loss
Selective Repeat can buffer correctly received out-of-order frames
Selective Repeat typically needs per-frame timers or equivalent retransmission tracking
questions.explanation: Go-Back-N usually discards out-of-order frames and retransmits from the missing one onward. Selective Repeat buffers out-of-order frames and retransmits only missing or damaged frames.
options: Go-Back-N may retransmit multiple frames after one loss
Selective Repeat can buffer correctly received out-of-order frames
Selective Repeat typically needs per-frame timers or equivalent retransmission tracking
Go-Back-N buffers every out-of-order frame by default

questions.prompt: Which mechanisms are required or commonly used by Selective Repeat ARQ?
answer: Receiver buffering for out-of-order frames
Individual acknowledgments or equivalent per-frame status
Selective retransmission of missing or corrupted frames
questions.explanation: Selective Repeat retains valid out-of-order frames and tracks acknowledgment status per frame. It retransmits only frames that need recovery rather than discarding all later data.
options: Receiver buffering for out-of-order frames
Individual acknowledgments or equivalent per-frame status
Selective retransmission of missing or corrupted frames
A missing frame must cause all later correct frames to be discarded permanently

questions.prompt: A Go-Back-N sender uses a 3-bit sequence number and a window size of 7. How many distinct sequence numbers exist?
questions.explanation: A 3-bit sequence number has 2^3=8 distinct values, numbered modulo 8. The Go-Back-N window of 7 is one less than this space.

questions.prompt: Which statements about cumulative acknowledgments in Go-Back-N are correct?
answer: An ACK can indicate the next expected sequence number
One ACK can acknowledge a prefix of frames
The receiver normally discards out-of-order frames
questions.explanation: Cumulative ACKs advance the acknowledged prefix by naming the next expected frame. Frames beyond a gap are generally discarded by a Go-Back-N receiver.
options: An ACK can indicate the next expected sequence number
One ACK can acknowledge a prefix of frames
The receiver normally discards out-of-order frames
The receiver accepts every out-of-order frame and delivers it immediately

questions.prompt: A Go-Back-N receiver expects frame 5 but receives frame 6. What does a standard receiver usually do?
options: Discard frame 6 and repeat the acknowledgment for the next expected frame
Buffer frame 6 and deliver it immediately
Advance the expected sequence to 7
Treat frame 6 as an Ethernet address
answer: Discard frame 6 and repeat the acknowledgment for the next expected frame
questions.explanation: Go-Back-N receivers accept only the next in-order frame. They discard frame 6 and typically send a duplicate cumulative ACK indicating that frame 5 is still expected.

questions.prompt: Which mechanisms are associated with reliable data-link ARQ?
answer: Error detection
Acknowledgments
Timeouts and retransmissions
questions.explanation: ARQ combines error detection with feedback and retransmission to recover lost or corrupted frames. Route aggregation is unrelated network-layer addressing functionality.
options: Error detection
Acknowledgments
Timeouts and retransmissions
Sequence numbers alone guarantee delivery despite loss

questions.prompt: A stop-and-wait protocol has data transmission time T_t and one-way propagation delay T_p. With negligible ACK transmission and processing, what is the cycle time?
options: T_t+2T_p
T_t+T_p
2T_t+T_p
2T_t+2T_p
answer: T_t+2T_p
questions.explanation: After transmitting for T_t, the sender waits for the data to propagate to the receiver and the ACK to propagate back, adding approximately 2T_p.

questions.prompt: A stop-and-wait sender spends most of each cycle idle on a long-delay link. Which architectural change most directly addresses this inefficiency?
answer: Allow multiple unacknowledged frames using a sliding window
questions.explanation: A sliding window pipelines several frames while feedback is in transit. This keeps the link busy when the bandwidth-delay product exceeds one frame.
options: Allow multiple unacknowledged frames using a sliding window
Increase the propagation distance
Reduce the sequence-number space to one value
Disable error detection

questions.prompt: A sliding-window sender can transmit W frames per RTT, each with L bits, over a link of rate R. Ignoring ACK overhead, what upper bound does the window impose on throughput?
options: min(R, WL/RTT)
R+WL/RTT
RTT/(WL)
W+L+R
answer: min(R, WL/RTT)
questions.explanation: The window can sustain at most WL bits per round trip, while the physical link limits rate to R. Throughput is bounded by the smaller of these values.

questions.prompt: A sender has a window of 8 frames, each 1000 bits, and RTT is 20 ms. What window-limited rate is available in Mb/s?
questions.explanation: The window carries 8,000 bits per 0.020 s, giving 400,000 bits/s=0.4 Mb/s.

questions.prompt: Which changes can improve stop-and-wait link utilization?
answer: Increase the number of outstanding frames with a sliding window
Reduce RTT
Increase frame size relative to RTT
questions.explanation: Utilization improves when more data can be sent before feedback returns, when RTT shrinks, or when each transmission occupies a larger share of the cycle. Greater propagation delay lowers utilization.
options: Increase the number of outstanding frames with a sliding window
Reduce RTT
Increase frame size relative to RTT
Increase RTT while keeping frame size and window fixed

questions.prompt: Which changes increase the fraction of time a stop-and-wait sender is waiting for acknowledgment rather than transmitting?
answer: Increase round-trip propagation time
Decrease frame transmission time while RTT stays fixed
Add ACK processing time
questions.explanation: The idle portion grows when feedback takes longer or data serialization becomes shorter. Increasing transmission time makes sending occupy a larger fraction of the cycle.
options: Increase round-trip propagation time
Decrease frame transmission time while RTT stays fixed
Add ACK processing time
Decrease RTT while keeping transmission and ACK processing times fixed

questions.prompt: An alternating-bit protocol has a 1-bit sequence number. How many distinct sequence values does it use?
questions.explanation: A one-bit sequence field represents values 0 and 1, so it has two distinct sequence values.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the alternating-bit protocol are correct?
answer: It is stop-and-wait ARQ
Sequence numbers alternate between 0 and 1
It helps detect duplicate retransmissions
questions.explanation: The protocol permits one outstanding frame and alternates a one-bit sequence number. The receiver uses it to distinguish a new frame from a retransmitted duplicate.
options: It is stop-and-wait ARQ
Sequence numbers alternate between 0 and 1
It helps detect duplicate retransmissions
The sequence number must increase modulo 8

questions.prompt: A sender's timeout is set shorter than the normal round-trip time. What failure can result?
options: Premature retransmissions of frames that are still in transit
The link rate becomes zero
All frames become correctly acknowledged without delay
The receiver's sequence space doubles
answer: Premature retransmissions of frames that are still in transit
questions.explanation: If the timeout expires before a valid ACK can normally return, the sender retransmits unnecessarily, causing duplicate traffic and possibly duplicate delivery unless sequence numbers handle it.

questions.prompt: An ACK is generated 2 ms after a frame arrives. The data frame takes 3 ms to transmit, 5 ms to propagate one way, and the ACK takes 5 ms to return by propagation. What is the time from transmission start until ACK arrival, ignoring ACK serialization?
questions.explanation: The timeline is 3 ms data transmission, 5 ms forward propagation, 2 ms ACK generation, and 5 ms return propagation. The total is 15 ms.

questions.prompt: In slotted ALOHA, a frame succeeds when how many stations transmit in a slot?
options: Exactly one
At least one
Exactly two
No stations
answer: Exactly one
questions.explanation: A collision occurs if multiple stations transmit in the same slot. A successful slot contains exactly one transmission.

questions.prompt: For slotted ALOHA with offered load G=1, compute throughput S=Ge^(−G) to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: At G=1, S=e^(−1)=1/e≈0.367879, which rounds to 0.368 frames per slot.

questions.prompt: At what offered load is slotted ALOHA throughput G e^(−G) maximized?
questions.explanation: Differentiating S(G)=Ge^(−G) gives S'=e^(−G)(1−G). The maximum occurs at G=1, with throughput 1/e.

questions.prompt: Which statements compare pure and slotted ALOHA?
answer: Slotted ALOHA requires slot synchronization
Pure ALOHA permits transmission at any time
The maximum normalized throughput of slotted ALOHA is 1/e
questions.explanation: Slotted ALOHA constrains starts to slot boundaries and has a one-frame vulnerable period; pure ALOHA's vulnerable period is two frame times, reducing its maximum throughput.
options: Slotted ALOHA requires slot synchronization
Pure ALOHA permits transmission at any time
The maximum normalized throughput of slotted ALOHA is 1/e
Pure ALOHA requires global slot synchronization

questions.prompt: For pure ALOHA, maximum normalized throughput is 1/(2e). Approximate it to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: 1/(2e)≈0.18394, which rounds to 0.184 successful frames per frame time.

questions.prompt: A station senses a busy CSMA medium. What is the basic principle of carrier sensing?
options: Defer transmission while the medium is busy
Transmit immediately to create a collision
Turn the frame into a circuit
Change the destination MAC address
answer: Defer transmission while the medium is busy
questions.explanation: Carrier sensing checks whether the medium is occupied. A station typically waits when it detects an ongoing transmission, reducing collisions compared with unsensed access.

questions.prompt: Why can collisions still occur in CSMA even when stations listen before transmitting?
answer: Propagation delay means two distant stations may both sense an idle medium
A transmission takes time to become observable everywhere
Two stations may begin nearly simultaneously
questions.explanation: A signal takes time to propagate. Before one station's transmission reaches another, both may observe idle and start, producing a collision.
options: Propagation delay means two distant stations may both sense an idle medium
A transmission takes time to become observable everywhere
Two stations may begin nearly simultaneously
Carrier sensing makes simultaneous starts impossible at any propagation delay

questions.prompt: In CSMA/CD, what does a transmitting station do after detecting a collision?
options: Abort the frame and send a jam signal before backing off
Continue transmitting silently until completion
Immediately declare the frame delivered
Switch to a different IP address
answer: Abort the frame and send a jam signal before backing off
questions.explanation: Collision detection causes a station to stop the current frame, signal the collision with a jam sequence, and wait a randomized backoff interval before retrying.

questions.prompt: Classic Ethernet at 10 Mb/s uses a slot time of 51.2 microseconds. How many bits can be transmitted during one slot time?
questions.explanation: 10,000,000 bits/s×51.2×10^−6 s=512 bits per slot time.

questions.prompt: Why must Ethernet's minimum frame transmission time be at least the round-trip propagation time of the collision domain in CSMA/CD?
options: The sender must still be transmitting when a worst-case collision signal returns
It ensures propagation delay is zero
It allows the receiver to choose an IP route
It eliminates the need for a CRC
answer: The sender must still be transmitting when a worst-case collision signal returns
questions.explanation: If a collision occurs at the far end, its signal needs a round-trip propagation time to reach the sender. The sender must still be transmitting then to detect the collision.

questions.prompt: Which statements about CSMA/CD are correct?
answer: It detects collisions while transmitting
It uses a backoff procedure after collisions
It is used by traditional shared, half-duplex Ethernet
questions.explanation: CSMA/CD is associated with shared half-duplex Ethernet. Full-duplex switched links have separate transmit and receive paths and do not use collision detection.
options: It detects collisions while transmitting
It uses a backoff procedure after collisions
It is used by traditional shared, half-duplex Ethernet
CSMA/CD is required on every full-duplex switched Ethernet link

questions.prompt: A 100 Mb/s Ethernet collision domain has a maximum round-trip propagation time of 5.12 microseconds. What minimum frame length in bits is required by the collision-detection timing condition?
questions.explanation: The frame time must cover the round trip: 100,000,000×5.12×10^−6=512 bits.

questions.prompt: In binary exponential backoff after the kth collision, the station chooses a random integer from which range, in the common Ethernet description?
options: 0 through 2^k−1, subject to a maximum exponent
1 through k
0 through k²
Exactly 2^k
answer: 0 through 2^k−1, subject to a maximum exponent
questions.explanation: The backoff window grows exponentially with the collision count. A random number of slot times is selected from 0 through 2^k−1, with the exponent capped.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Ethernet MAC addresses are correct?
answer: A MAC address is used for link-layer delivery on a local network
A broadcast MAC can reach all stations on a broadcast LAN
A router normally rewrites the link-layer addresses when forwarding to another link
questions.explanation: MAC addresses have local-link scope. Routers create a new frame on each outgoing link; IP addresses provide internetwork endpoint addressing.
options: A MAC address is used for link-layer delivery on a local network
A broadcast MAC can reach all stations on a broadcast LAN
A router normally rewrites the link-layer addresses when forwarding to another link
A router preserves the same source and destination MAC addresses across every routed hop

questions.prompt: A 48-bit Ethernet MAC address contains how many hexadecimal digits?
questions.explanation: Each hexadecimal digit represents four bits. A 48-bit address therefore has 48/4=12 hexadecimal digits.

questions.prompt: A 48-bit MAC address is written using two hexadecimal digits per byte. How many bytes are represented?
questions.explanation: There are eight bits per byte, so 48/8=6 bytes. Each byte is shown by two hexadecimal digits.

questions.prompt: Which fields are commonly present in an Ethernet II frame?
answer: Destination MAC address
Source MAC address
Type field
questions.explanation: Ethernet II includes destination and source MAC addresses and a Type field indicating the upper-layer protocol. TCP acknowledgment numbers reside in the transport header.
options: Destination MAC address
Source MAC address
Type field
An Ethernet II frame uses a hop-count field in place of the Type field

questions.prompt: A switch receives a frame whose destination MAC is unknown in its forwarding table. What does a learning Ethernet switch commonly do?
options: Flood it out other ports in the same VLAN except the incoming port
Drop it unconditionally
Route it using the destination IP
Send it only to the oldest learned port
answer: Flood it out other ports in the same VLAN except the incoming port
questions.explanation: For an unknown unicast destination, a switch floods the frame within the broadcast domain, excluding the port on which it arrived.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Ethernet switch learning are correct?
answer: The source MAC and incoming port can be learned from a frame
The forwarding database maps MAC addresses to ports
Aging can remove stale entries
questions.explanation: A switch learns from source MAC addresses and records the associated input port. Dynamic entries age out; ordinary Ethernet switching is based on MAC rather than physical-layer signal interpretation or IP routing.
options: The source MAC and incoming port can be learned from a frame
The forwarding database maps MAC addresses to ports
Aging can remove stale entries
A switch learns the destination port solely from the destination address of an incoming frame

questions.prompt: A stop-and-wait link sends 2000-bit frames at 2 Mb/s. RTT excluding data transmission is 18 ms, ACK transmission negligible. Find utilization percentage.
questions.explanation: Transmission time is 1 ms. Cycle time is 1+18=19 ms, so utilization is 1/19≈0.05263=5.26%.

questions.prompt: One-way propagation delay is 5 ms and frame transmission time is 1 ms. A sliding window has 11 frames. Under the standard window-filling condition, is this sufficient to keep the sender busy?
options: Yes; W=1+2a/Tt=11
No; at least 5 frames are needed
No; at least 21 frames are needed
No window can overcome propagation delay
answer: Yes; W=1+2a/Tt=11
questions.explanation: With a=5 ms and Tt=1 ms, the required window is 1+2a/Tt=1+10=11 frames. The stated window exactly meets the idealized condition.

questions.prompt: Which outcomes follow when a sender window is smaller than the number of frames needed to cover the bandwidth-delay product?
answer: The sender may become idle while waiting for acknowledgments
The link can be underutilized despite available capacity
Increasing the window can improve utilization up to the path limit
questions.explanation: An undersized window cannot keep enough data in flight to cover the feedback delay. Increasing it can raise utilization until the link or another bottleneck is saturated.
options: The sender may become idle while waiting for acknowledgments
The link can be underutilized despite available capacity
Increasing the window can improve utilization up to the path limit
A smaller sender window always increases link utilization

questions.prompt: Which statements about ARQ sequence-number spaces are correct?
answer: Sequence numbers wrap modulo the field's value range
Window constraints prevent old and new frames from becoming ambiguous
Selective Repeat needs a smaller maximum window than the full sequence space
questions.explanation: An m-bit sequence number has 2^m values and wraps modulo that space. Window limits ensure the receiver can distinguish delayed duplicates from new transmissions.
options: Sequence numbers wrap modulo the field's value range
Window constraints prevent old and new frames from becoming ambiguous
Selective Repeat needs a smaller maximum window than the full sequence space
Selective Repeat can use a window of the entire sequence-number space without ambiguity

questions.prompt: A two-bit Go-Back-N protocol uses sequence numbers modulo 4. Frames 2, 3, and 0 are sent. A cumulative ACK says the next expected frame is 0. How many of these frames remain unacknowledged?
questions.explanation: The ACK for next expected 0 confirms receipt of frames 2 and 3. Frame 0 is still outstanding, so one remains unacknowledged.

questions.prompt: Why is a Selective Repeat window limited to at most half of the sequence-number space?
answer: To prevent an old delayed frame from being mistaken for a new frame after wraparound
questions.explanation: If sender and receiver windows overlap across sequence-number wraparound, an old duplicate may appear to be a new frame. Keeping each window at most half the space avoids this ambiguity.
options: To prevent an old delayed frame from being mistaken for a new frame after wraparound
To make the link rate exactly twice the RTT
To force the sender to retransmit all frames
To avoid calculating checksums

questions.prompt: Which events are handled differently by Go-Back-N and Selective Repeat?
answer: Go-Back-N retransmits the missing frame and later outstanding frames
Selective Repeat can retransmit only the missing frame
Selective Repeat buffers out-of-order data frames
questions.explanation: Go-Back-N recovers by resending the suffix beginning at the missing frame. Selective Repeat buffers later frames and selectively retransmits the missing one.
options: Go-Back-N retransmits the missing frame and later outstanding frames
Selective Repeat can retransmit only the missing frame
Selective Repeat buffers out-of-order data frames
Go-Back-N buffers and individually acknowledges every out-of-order frame

questions.prompt: An ACK in Go-Back-N states that the receiver expects sequence number 7. What does this cumulative ACK normally imply?
options: All frames before 7 have been received in order
Only frame 7 has been received
No frame has been received
Frames 7 and later have been delivered
answer: All frames before 7 have been received in order
questions.explanation: A cumulative ACK for the next expected number indicates that the receiver has accepted every preceding frame in sequence.

questions.prompt: A sender transmits 4-bit Go-Back-N frames with sequence numbers 0 through 15. If the next expected sequence is 14, what sequence number follows 15?
questions.explanation: Sequence numbers wrap modulo 16. After 15, the next value is 0.

questions.prompt: Which statements about acknowledgments and retransmissions are correct?
answer: A duplicate ACK can indicate a missing earlier frame
Timeouts can trigger retransmission
Sequence numbers help suppress duplicate delivery
questions.explanation: Repeated cumulative acknowledgments often signal a gap; timers recover when feedback is absent. Sequence numbers let receivers recognize duplicate frames, while ACKs are separate control messages.
options: A duplicate ACK can indicate a missing earlier frame
Timeouts can trigger retransmission
Sequence numbers help suppress duplicate delivery
A duplicate ACK proves that the reverse path has no packet loss

questions.prompt: In a link protocol with bit errors, why is a checksum or CRC added to each frame?
options: To detect corruption before accepting the frame
To guarantee the frame is delivered
To encrypt the payload
To choose the next hop
answer: To detect corruption before accepting the frame
questions.explanation: Error-detection bits allow the receiver to identify many corrupted frames. Detection alone does not guarantee delivery; ARQ may be used for recovery.

questions.prompt: A 1200-byte payload has a 4-byte CRC field and a 6-byte framing header. What is the total frame length?
questions.explanation: The frame consists of 1200 payload bytes plus 4 CRC bytes and 6 header bytes: 1210 bytes.

questions.prompt: Which statements about checksums and CRCs are correct?
answer: They add redundancy for error detection
They can detect but not necessarily correct errors
CRC operates on polynomial representations over GF(2)
questions.explanation: Checksums and CRCs detect corruption by adding check bits; correction needs additional coding or retransmission. Some error patterns can yield a valid check value, so passing is not absolute proof.
options: They add redundancy for error detection
They can detect but not necessarily correct errors
CRC operates on polynomial representations over GF(2)
A CRC can always reconstruct the original corrupted bits without retransmission

questions.prompt: Which error patterns are guaranteed to be detected by a degree-r CRC generator?
answer: Every nonzero burst error of length at most r
questions.explanation: A degree-r generator guarantees detection of all nonzero burst errors up to length r. Some longer error polynomials are multiples of the generator and can be undetected.
options: Every nonzero burst error of length at most r
Every burst error of length r+1
Every error pattern containing an even number of bit flips
Only burst errors whose length is exactly r

questions.prompt: A received CRC codeword has a nonzero remainder under the agreed generator. What is the correct interpretation?
answer: The receiver detected an error
questions.explanation: A nonzero remainder means the received polynomial is not divisible by the agreed generator, so the CRC check detects corruption.
options: The receiver detected an error
The sender used an even number of bits
The frame is guaranteed correct
The generator degree is zero

questions.prompt: Which statements about error-detecting codes are correct?
answer: A valid codeword is selected from a subset of all bit strings
Redundancy can make some corrupted strings invalid
Some error patterns can transform one valid codeword into another
questions.explanation: Coding redundancy separates valid codewords, enabling detection or correction within distance limits. A corruption may land on another codeword, and detection alone does not correct it.
options: A valid codeword is selected from a subset of all bit strings
Redundancy can make some corrupted strings invalid
Some error patterns can transform one valid codeword into another
Every possible bit string is a valid codeword when redundancy is added

questions.prompt: A code's minimum distance is 4. Which pair of guarantees is valid?
options: Detect 3 errors and correct 1
Detect 4 errors and correct 2
Detect 2 errors and correct 2
Detect 1 error and correct 3
answer: Detect 3 errors and correct 1
questions.explanation: Detection is guaranteed through d−1=3 errors, and correction through floor((4−1)/2)=1 error.

questions.prompt: A parity code adds one bit to 7 data bits. What is the resulting codeword length?
questions.explanation: One parity bit is appended to the seven data bits, producing an 8-bit codeword.

questions.prompt: Which statements about a single parity bit are correct?
answer: It detects every odd number of flipped bits
It can fail to detect two flipped bits
It adds one bit of redundancy
questions.explanation: Parity checks only whether the total number of 1s has the required parity. It detects odd-weight errors but gives no location information, and two flips preserve parity.
options: It detects every odd number of flipped bits
It can fail to detect two flipped bits
It adds one bit of redundancy
A single parity bit detects every pattern with an even number of flips

questions.prompt: In Ethernet CSMA/CD, why does the jam signal follow collision detection?
options: To ensure all stations on the collision domain recognize the collision
To acknowledge successful delivery
To reserve the channel permanently
To encode the IP destination
answer: To ensure all stations on the collision domain recognize the collision
questions.explanation: The jam sequence makes the collision event sufficiently noticeable across the shared medium before stations enter backoff.

questions.prompt: A shared Ethernet has a slot time of 51.2 microseconds. At 100 Mb/s, how many bits are transmitted during one slot?
questions.explanation: 100,000,000×51.2×10^−6=5,120 bits are transmitted in one slot interval.

questions.prompt: Which properties are associated with switched full-duplex Ethernet?
answer: A dedicated point-to-point link can carry simultaneous send and receive traffic
Collisions are not expected on a full-duplex link
CSMA/CD is unnecessary
questions.explanation: Full-duplex switched links separate transmit and receive paths between a host and switch. They do not use the shared-medium collision mechanism.
options: A dedicated point-to-point link can carry simultaneous send and receive traffic
Collisions are not expected on a full-duplex link
CSMA/CD is unnecessary
Full-duplex switched links use collision backoff independently in both directions

questions.prompt: A station has experienced several consecutive collisions. What effect does binary exponential backoff have?
options: It expands the random backoff window as collisions accumulate
It forces immediate retransmission every time
It reduces the frame's CRC length
It permanently blocks the station
answer: It expands the random backoff window as collisions accumulate
questions.explanation: Increasing the contention window after repeated collisions reduces the chance that the same stations retransmit simultaneously again.

questions.prompt: Which statements about ALOHA protocols are correct?
answer: Pure ALOHA allows transmission at arbitrary times
Slotted ALOHA restricts transmissions to slot boundaries
Slotted ALOHA has a shorter vulnerable period than pure ALOHA
questions.explanation: Slotted operation aligns frame starts and reduces the vulnerable period from two frame times to one. Both remain random-access protocols and can collide.
options: Pure ALOHA allows transmission at arbitrary times
Slotted ALOHA restricts transmissions to slot boundaries
Slotted ALOHA has a shorter vulnerable period than pure ALOHA
Pure ALOHA has half the vulnerable period of slotted ALOHA

questions.prompt: Classic Ethernet operates at 100 Mb/s. The maximum one-way propagation delay is 25.6 microseconds. What minimum frame size in bytes is needed to ensure a sender is still transmitting when a worst-case collision returns? Ignore jam bits.
questions.explanation: The round-trip propagation time is 51.2 microseconds. At 100 Mb/s, 5120 bits can be transmitted during that interval, which is 640 bytes.

questions.prompt: For pure ALOHA, the vulnerable period for a frame of duration T is
options: T
2T
answer: 2T
questions.explanation: A frame can collide with another that starts up to T before or T after its start. The total vulnerable interval is 2T.

questions.prompt: Which statements about CSMA persistence strategies are correct?
answer: 1-persistent transmits immediately when the medium becomes idle
Nonpersistent waits a random time after sensing busy
p-persistent applies probabilistic transmission at slot boundaries
questions.explanation: The variants define how a station behaves when it senses a busy or idle channel. Propagation can still cause collisions, so none eliminates them entirely.
options: 1-persistent transmits immediately when the medium becomes idle
Nonpersistent waits a random time after sensing busy
p-persistent applies probabilistic transmission at slot boundaries
Nonpersistent CSMA transmits continuously while the channel is busy

questions.prompt: A link's one-way propagation delay is 4 microseconds and rate is 25 Mb/s. What frame size in bits has transmission time equal to the round-trip propagation time?
questions.explanation: Round-trip propagation is 8 microseconds. Multiply by 25×10^6 bits/s to get 200 bits.

questions.prompt: An Ethernet collision domain has round-trip propagation time 40 microseconds at 10 Mb/s. What minimum frame size satisfies the collision-detection timing condition?
options: 40 bits
100 bits
400 bits
4000 bits
answer: 400 bits
questions.explanation: The minimum frame transmission time must cover the 40-microsecond round trip. At 10 Mb/s, that is 10,000,000×40×10^−6=400 bits.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Ethernet framing and collision handling are correct?
answer: The frame check sequence detects many transmission errors
The minimum frame size supports collision detection in classic Ethernet
Backoff randomizes retransmission timing after collision
questions.explanation: Ethernet uses an FCS for error detection, a minimum frame size related to collision timing, and backoff after collisions. The interframe gap is timing, not an address field.
options: The frame check sequence detects many transmission errors
The minimum frame size supports collision detection in classic Ethernet
Backoff randomizes retransmission timing after collision
Ethernet backoff guarantees that a collision never occurs again

questions.prompt: A 1500-byte Ethernet payload is sent in a frame with 18 bytes of header and trailer overhead. How many total bytes are carried, ignoring preamble and interframe gap?
questions.explanation: Add the payload and stated overhead: 1500+18=1518 bytes.

questions.prompt: A receiver gets a frame with a CRC remainder that is nonzero. What should it conclude?
options: An error has been detected and the frame should not be accepted as valid
The frame is certainly correct
The destination MAC is unknown
The sender has received an ACK
answer: An error has been detected and the frame should not be accepted as valid
questions.explanation: A nonzero syndrome indicates that the received bit sequence fails the CRC check. The receiver treats it as corrupted and discards it or requests retransmission per protocol.

questions.prompt: A 4-bit CRC remainder is appended to a 100-bit dataword. What is the resulting codeword length?
questions.explanation: The codeword includes the original 100 data bits plus 4 CRC bits, totaling 104 bits.

questions.prompt: Which statements about a sliding-window link protocol are correct?
answer: It can keep multiple frames in flight
It can improve utilization on a long-RTT link
It requires sequence numbers to identify frames
questions.explanation: Sliding windows pipeline frames and use sequence numbers to track outstanding data. Reliable ARQ still uses acknowledgments or equivalent feedback.
options: It can keep multiple frames in flight
It can improve utilization on a long-RTT link
It requires sequence numbers to identify frames
A sliding window permits only one unacknowledged frame at a time

questions.prompt: A 5-bit sequence number field is used. What is the sequence-number space size?
questions.explanation: An m-bit field represents 2^m values. For m=5, there are 32 sequence numbers.

questions.prompt: A Go-Back-N receiver expects frame 7 in a modulo-8 sequence space, but receives frame 0 before frame 7. What does it normally do?
answer: Discard frame 0 and repeat the ACK for frame 7
questions.explanation: Go-Back-N accepts only the next in-order frame. Since 7 is missing, frame 0 is out of order and is discarded; the receiver indicates that 7 is still expected.
options: Discard frame 0 and repeat the ACK for frame 7
Buffer frame 0 and deliver it immediately
Advance expectation to frame 1
Acknowledge every frame through 0

questions.prompt: A Selective Repeat receiver has an in-window frame 0 arrive before missing frame 7, with sequence numbers modulo 8. What can it do?
options: Buffer and acknowledge frame 0 while waiting for frame 7
Discard frame 0 because every protocol is Go-Back-N
Deliver frame 0 before all preceding data
Reset the sender window
answer: Buffer and acknowledge frame 0 while waiting for frame 7
questions.explanation: Selective Repeat can accept an in-window out-of-order frame, store it, and acknowledge it individually. Ordered delivery can resume after frame 7 fills the gap.

questions.prompt: Which statements about error detection versus error correction are correct?
answer: Detection can indicate corruption without identifying the original bits
Correction requires enough redundancy to infer the intended codeword
ARQ can recover by retransmission after detecting an error
questions.explanation: Detection flags invalid data; correction needs sufficient code distance to identify the transmitted codeword. One parity bit detects a single-bit error but cannot locate which bit flipped.
options: Detection can indicate corruption without identifying the original bits
Correction requires enough redundancy to infer the intended codeword
ARQ can recover by retransmission after detecting an error
Error detection always identifies the exact positions of all corrupted bits

questions.prompt: An even-parity receiver sees data plus parity containing an odd number of 1s. What can it conclude?
options: A parity error is detected
The exact error location is known
The data is correct
Two bits definitely flipped
answer: A parity error is detected
questions.explanation: An odd count violates the even-parity rule, so an error is detected. Parity alone cannot determine the error location or number of flipped bits.

questions.prompt: A codeword is changed by flipping exactly one bit. Which additional property is needed to guarantee that the receiver can identify and correct the flipped bit?
answer: A code with minimum distance at least 3
questions.explanation: Correcting one error requires disjoint radius-one decoding neighborhoods, which needs minimum distance 2t+1=3. A parity bit can detect a single error but cannot locate it.
options: A code with minimum distance at least 3
A single parity bit only
A code with minimum distance 2
No redundancy

questions.prompt: Which statements summarize reliable data-link communication?
answer: Frames can be protected with error-detection bits
Acknowledgments provide receiver feedback
Retransmissions can recover from loss or detected corruption
questions.explanation: Reliable link protocols combine detection and feedback with retransmission. They can recover from many errors but cannot ensure the physical medium never produces errors.
options: Frames can be protected with error-detection bits
Acknowledgments provide receiver feedback
Retransmissions can recover from loss or detected corruption
Acknowledgments eliminate the need for sequence numbers and duplicate suppression
